## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Every instruction counts the same: the hardware float instructions
  (`-mfprev1`) too, divide included. fwtest computes them as IEEE 754
  single precision, rounding to nearest even and keeping subnormals; no
  float condition raises an exception or sets a flag (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`,
  HW-63, gives the edge cases).
- Once released, core 1 also runs one instruction a cycle. The cores take
  turns: core 0 runs 1024 instructions, then core 1 as many cycles as
  passed. They share memory with no caches and no contention, so neither
  slows the other, but a store by one core reaches the other core's loads
  up to one turn (1024 cycles) later. Core 1 takes the interrupts its own
  enable words enable (HW-64).
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

### Timers and their acknowledge

The write to a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register that acknowledges its
interrupt also restarts that timer's count and its period from the moment
of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.
## Outputs

All in `--out`. A run writes only what it was asked for, plus
`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |
| `lcd-WHEN.png` | The screen, 240 x 240, 8-bit RGB, whatever the display's on/off state. Each pixel is the panel's 16-bit colour (5-6-5 bits) with each channel scaled to 8 bits (`c * 255 / 31`, or `/ 63` for green). |
| `leds.csv` | Header `ms,led0,...,led40`, then one row per sample: the sample's time, and for each LED the share of the time since the previous sample (or since the start) that it was lit, in thousandths (0 to 1000, rounded). LED N belongs to key N. |
| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `midi-out.csv` | Header `ms,byte`, then one row per byte the MIDI output sent: the time its stop bit ended (ms, three decimals) and the byte as two hex digits. Empty but for the header if nothing was sent. |
| `midi-out.txt` | The same bytes as MIDI messages, one a line: the time of the message's last byte, then the message ("MIDI output"). |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |
| `junit.xml` | JUnit XML: a test case `run` (fails on a fault or hang, and on a halt without `--halt-ok`), and one `golden NAME` per golden file. |

`result.json` holds: `fwtest` (version and the emulator build it carries),
`image` (file name, size, SHA-256), `script_sha256`, `run` (`outcome`,
`detail`, `emulated_ms`, `instructions` per core, `midi_bytes_dropped`,
`midi_out_bytes_dropped`,
`unmodelled_accesses`, and every output's name, size and SHA-256), `golden`
(each file's `match` or `mismatch` and why), and `exit_code`.

- `midi_bytes_dropped`: bytes that arrived while the image had no MIDI
  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.
  `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-71, says what counts as set up: the receiver
  takes bytes only by DMA into a ring, so a byte that arrives without one
  is dropped and raises nothing. The bytes' pace doesn't depend on the
  baud rate, the UART clock or the pins, which fwtest ignores.
- `midi_out_bytes_dropped`: bytes the image wrote to the MIDI output
  while its UART was off (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-74); they were not sent.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## MIDI output

fwtest models the MIDI OUT of the FM-1's sibling, the SMK-37: the transmit
side of the UART that receives the MIDI input (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-72
to HW-74, says which registers). A real FM-1 has no MIDI OUT jack, so on
the FM-1 itself these bytes go nowhere; the SMK-37 sends them through its
3.5 mm jack.

- **What goes out.** Writing the transmit count sends that many bytes from
  RAM, read at the moment of the write; writing the data register sends
  one byte. Each byte takes 320 µs on the wire (31 250 baud, whatever the
  baud and clock registers hold). A transfer started while another is
  still going waits behind it, byte for byte.
- **When it's done.** When the last byte has gone, the transmit pending
  flag is set and, if its interrupt is enabled, the UART's interrupt
  source is raised (HW-74). With the UART off nothing is sent:
  `result.json` counts the bytes in `midi_out_bytes_dropped`.
- **The capture** (`--midi-out`). `midi-out.csv` holds every byte sent,
  in order, with the time its stop bit ended: exact, at the emulated
  clock, whether core 0 is busy or waiting. `midi-out.txt` decodes them

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Every instruction counts the same: the hardware float instructions
  (`-mfprev1`) too, divide included. fwtest computes them as IEEE 754
  single precision, rounding to nearest even and keeping subnormals; no
  float condition raises an exception or sets a flag (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`,
  HW-63, gives the edge cases).
- Once released, core 1 also runs one instruction a cycle. The cores take
  turns: core 0 runs 1024 instructions, then core 1 as many cycles as
  passed. They share memory with no caches and no contention, so neither
  slows the other, but a store by one core reaches the other core's loads
  up to one turn (1024 cycles) later. Core 1 takes the interrupts its own
  enable words enable (HW-64).
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

### Timers and their acknowledge

The write to a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register that acknowledges its
interrupt also restarts that timer's count and its period from the moment
of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.
## Outputs

All in `--out`. A run writes only what it was asked for, plus
`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |
| `lcd-WHEN.png` | The screen, 240 x 240, 8-bit RGB, whatever the display's on/off state. Each pixel is the panel's 16-bit colour (5-6-5 bits) with each channel scaled to 8 bits (`c * 255 / 31`, or `/ 63` for green). |
| `leds.csv` | Header `ms,led0,...,led40`, then one row per sample: the sample's time, and for each LED the share of the time since the previous sample (or since the start) that it was lit, in thousandths (0 to 1000, rounded). LED N belongs to key N. |
| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `midi-out.csv` | Header `ms,byte`, then one row per byte the MIDI output sent: the time its stop bit ended (ms, three decimals) and the byte as two hex digits. Empty but for the header if nothing was sent. |
| `midi-out.txt` | The same bytes as MIDI messages, one a line: the time of the message's last byte, then the message ("MIDI output"). |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |
| `junit.xml` | JUnit XML: a test case `run` (fails on a fault or hang, and on a halt without `--halt-ok`), and one `golden NAME` per golden file. |

`result.json` holds: `fwtest` (version and the emulator build it carries),
`image` (file name, size, SHA-256), `script_sha256`, `run` (`outcome`,
`detail`, `emulated_ms`, `instructions` per core, `midi_bytes_dropped`,
`midi_out_bytes_dropped`,
`unmodelled_accesses`, and every output's name, size and SHA-256), `golden`

  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

### M6a: MIDI in (firmware side)
- Status 2026-10-24 (session M6a, firmware side, on the owner's Mac): done,
  in pull requests #74 (start), #75 (SR-7's workaround removed), #76
  (spec request SR-8), #79 (the build's last instruction guard removed,
  fwtest 0.4.0) and the MIDI pull request (the parser, the engine's side,
  the receiver and the tests), which builds on SR-8's answer (#81).
  - **The receiver** (HW-67 to HW-71): the MIDI IN jack's UART1, by DMA
    into a ring, read once a block from the engine's callback; no
    interrupt. The chip's baud rate, clock and pin are still open (Q-12)
    and set only with real hardware.
  - **The parser** (our own, MIDI 1.0's rules; tools/midi_model.py is the
    same rules again for the tests): running status, realtime anywhere,
    SysEx skipped at any length, junk dropped and counted.
  - **The engine's side**: notes held apart by the panel, MIDI and the
    sustain pedal, so neither ends the other's; velocity, pitch bend (2
    semitones, RPN 0 up to 24), vibrato on the mod wheel, volume and
    expression, all notes off, all sound off, program change, mono and
    poly; a receive channel (omni by default) and a controller map in a
    versioned settings struct for M7 to save and M8 to extend; MIDI's
    notes on the panel screen.
  - **Tests**: nine fwtest MIDI cases from generated scripts, each byte
    stream checked against the model; bends within 0.002 semitones,
    vibrato ±0.49, volume and expression on their curve, all sound off
    silent within 6 ms, sustain at five times, channel 10 only, panel and
    MIDI together without stuck notes (golden screen), a full wire for
    6 s without a drop or underrun. R-MIDI-1 to R-MIDI-7.
  - **Figures** (fwtest): latency 1.7 to 2.9 ms from a note's last byte to
    its first sample (at most two blocks); at rest +2.0% (36 instructions a
    block), loaded +1.0%; code 18 408 bytes, static RAM 143 256: the M5
    budgets hold, none raised.
  - **The owner's decisions** (2026-10-24): the loaded measure includes
    MIDI (#86's M6 budgets, #87's script: 109 899 a block of 131 072);
    a program change and the mono and poly messages release held notes,
    as PRESETS does, by design.
  - **Open items:**
    - **The receiver on the chip.** HW-70 (the receive set-up bits) is
      known from the emulator only, and the baud rate, UART clock, pin
      and port set-up are not set (Q-12). The receiver also writes
      UART1's `CON0` once a block to latch the byte count (HW-69); what
      that write does on the chip, beyond the latch, is not known. To
      settle with real hardware (Level 2) or a further spec request.
    - **The dense case the prompt named can't happen on the wire.** At
      31 250 baud a block (1.45 ms) carries about 4.5 bytes, two notes
      in running status, so "all 16 voices struck again every block"
      can't arrive by MIDI. The test (mididense) and the loaded measure
      fill the wire instead (all 16 voices sounding, notes struck again
      continuously); a faster input (USB MIDI, M11) could come closer.
  - **Next: M6b, MIDI out**, waiting on the spec side (which port the FM-1
    sends MIDI on; the spec side has #82 open on MIDI output).

### M1 to M9 (firmware side)
- **M1** boot: clocks, interrupts, timer (done; above).
- **M2** screen (done; above).
- **M3** keys, encoders, pot, LEDs (done; above).
- **M4** audio (done; above). **M4b** a platform test: Plaits (MIT) as
  a demo build, and the loaded-case budget (done; above).
- **M5** the FM engine (done; above).
- **M6a** MIDI in (done; above). **M6b** MIDI out (next, waiting on the
  spec side).
- **M7** flash storage.
- **M8** UI and original presets (no Yamaha factory voices).
- **M9** packaging, and a raw-image boot path in the app.

### Level 2: real hardware
- **M10** recovery kit.
- **M11** USB-MIDI and the update handler.
- **M12** hardware checklist.

## Risks

# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# The firmware's fwtest suite (docs/HARNESS.md, "Suites"). tools/fw-suite.py
# puts the image under test at out/fw/app.bin and the test images (the same
# source built with one SB_TEST_* define each) beside it, runs this suite
# through tools/fwtest, and then checks the captures: its docstring says how.
#
# boot (R-BOOT-1, R-BOOT-4, R-BOOT-5, R-CLK-1, R-IRQ-1, R-IRQ-2): main runs,
#   writes the marker and the console line, measures the clock and starts
#   the tick; RAM from 0x01c7fc00 to the vector table is as fwtest started
#   it (the r0 block, then zeros): golden files, exact. The beacon and the
#   vector table are checked by tools/fw-suite.py (the table against the
#   ELF's symbols, so a code change doesn't need a new golden file).
# heartbeat, heartbeat2 (R-BOOT-2, R-BOOT-3, R-BOOT-4, R-IRQ-1, R-IRQ-2):
#   1.25 and 2.25 s on the tick, the beacon captured along the way; the
#   watchdog fails the run if the beat count stops for 5 ms. The two differ
#   only in length, so their difference is the steady state (since M2).
# screen (R-LCD-1 to R-LCD-4): the address pattern at 300 ms, the test
#   screen at 800 ms and, one heartbeat later, at 1 500 ms: golden images,
#   exact, and tools/fw-suite.py checks every pixel of the pattern and the
#   test screen's border, corners and ramps on its own.
# flood (R-LCD-5): a test build sends whole frames back to back once the
#   test screen is up; every tick must keep its timing.
# fault (R-IRQ-4): a test build overruns main's stack; the next tick finds
#   the guard overwritten, reports it on the console and halts.
# stray (R-IRQ-3): a test build raises an interrupt nothing handles; its
#   stub reports the source on the console and halts.
# badinsn (a limit of the harness, no requirement): an undecodable
#   instruction ends the run with fwtest's own fault, before any handler of
#   ours could run (SR-1).
# Since M3, the panel's controls and LEDs (scripts in tests/fw/scripts/;
# the input record at 0x01c00060 holds the events, tools/fw-suite.py
# checks them and compares them with tests/fw/events/<case>.txt):
# keys (R-KEY-1, R-KEY-2, R-LED-1, R-LED-3, R-INPUT-1): every key and
#   button alone: the right control, debounce latency, its LED lit while
#   held and no other.
# chords (R-KEY-2, R-KEY-3, R-ENC-1, R-INPUT-2, R-LCD-6): chords, a
#   would-be ghost, keys held in the encoders' columns, chatter, a glitch;
#   the panel screen against a golden image (since M5 at 1 050 ms, one
#   frame after the last change it shows, not 1 030: the panel is drawn
#   in frames).
# encoders (R-ENC-1, R-ENC-2, R-INPUT-3): slow, fast, shared columns, all
#   seven at once with a chord and a pot sweep; every tick still on time.
# pot (R-POT-1, R-POT-2): steps, the ends, noise at rest, a sweep.
# leds (R-LED-2): a test build sets each LED to its own brightness.
# ledshow (R-LED-3): the keys script on a test build whose scan times when
#   it first drives an LED main has just set.
# Since M4, audio (--wav, --ipb; the audio record at 0x01c00550; our own
# analysis, tools/audio_analysis.py):
# tone (R-AUD-1, R-AUD-4): the test tone's frequency, level and THD+N, a
#   clean start and stop, and silence at rest around it.
# notes (R-AUD-2, R-AUD-5, R-AUD-6): single notes' pitch, level (MASTER),
#   latency from the key and from its event, no clicks, silence between.
# audioload (R-AUD-1, R-AUD-3, R-INPUT-3, R-FM-6): 10.9 s of the heaviest
#   input (since M5 the FM engine's: test patch 6 on all 16 voices, 20 keys
#   struck again in turn, six encoders, MASTER, the tone): no underrun,
#   every tick on time, both cores rendering.
# audiogold (R-AUD-7): a note and the tone, the whole output against a
#   golden WAV, exact. It moves whenever startup or the scan's timing
#   moves a note by a block (later milestones will): run the suite, check
#   that every other audio case passes, then copy audiogold/audio.wav
#   over golden/audiogold/audio.wav in the same commit.
# underrun (R-AUD-3): a test build late for one block in 64: each counted
#   and reported on the console, and the output goes on.
# Since M5, the FM engine (scripts fm*.txt; the engine's record at
# 0x01c00590; tools/fw-suite.py's checks, the test patches' values from
# tools/fm_patch.py). The notes case plays its test patch 0 since M5.
# fmbessel (R-FM-1): test patch 1's sidebands against Bessel functions.
# fmenv (R-FM-3): test patch 2's envelope stages, rates and levels.
# fmmono (R-FM-5): mono, legato and glide on test patch 3.
# fmsteal (R-FM-4): 17 notes held on 16 voices, one stolen, no click.
# fmvel (R-FM-3): a test build whose keys play five velocities.
# fmgold, fmgold2 (R-FM-8, R-FM-9): every test patch against a golden WAV,
#   twice: the same bytes both times. Regenerate it as audiogold's.
#
# NAME      EXPECT     IMAGE                          run options

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Writes the fwtest scripts of M6a's MIDI cases (tests/fw/scripts/midi*.txt;
R-MIDI-*), and reads their byte streams back for tools/fw-suite.py.

  midi_scripts.py            writes every script, and perfload.txt's MIDI part
  midi_scripts.py --check    exits 1 if a committed script differs

A `midi` event's bytes arrive one every 320 us, the first 320 us after its
time (docs/HARNESS.md, "Scripts"); the writer never lets two `midi`
events overlap, so the bytes reach the firmware in the order written.
Streams that are long or random (a SysEx flood, garbage, the dense
stream) come from a fixed seed, so the scripts are the same every time.
"""

import os
import sys

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SCRIPTS = os.path.join(ROOT, "tests", "fw", "scripts")
BYTE_MS = 0.32
CHUNK = 32          # bytes per `midi` line


class Script:
    def __init__(self, name, about):
        self.name, self.about, self.lines, self.t = name, about, [], 0.0

    def at(self, ms):
        """The next event no earlier than ms (and after the last byte)."""
        self.t = max(self.t, ms)
        return self

    def wait(self, ms):
        self.t += ms
        return self

    def midi(self, *data):
        b = [x for d in data for x in (d if isinstance(d, (list, tuple, bytes)) else [d])]
        for i in range(0, len(b), CHUNK):
            part = b[i:i + CHUNK]
            self.lines.append("%-8s midi %s" % (fmt(self.t), " ".join("%02x" % x for x in part)))
            self.t = round(self.t + BYTE_MS * len(part), 3)
        return self

    def event(self, text):
        self.lines.append("%-8s %s" % (fmt(self.t), text))
        return self

    def text(self):
        head = ["# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT", "# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98", "#",
                "# Written by tools/midi_scripts.py; don't edit by hand.", "#"]
        head += ["# " + l if l else "#" for l in self.about.split("\n")]
        return "\n".join(head + ["#", "# time   event"] + self.lines) + "\n"


def fmt(ms):
    s = "%.3f" % ms
    return s.rstrip("0").rstrip(".")


def rng(seed):
    x = seed
    while True:
        x = (x * 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7FFFFFFF
        yield x >> 16 & 0xFF


def on(note, vel, ch=0):
    return [0x90 | ch, note, vel]


def off(note, ch=0):
    return [0x80 | ch, note, 0x40]


def cc(n, v, ch=0):
    return [0xB0 | ch, n, v]

"""Runs the firmware's fwtest suite and checks what it captured (check

to R-LCD-5, and since M3 R-KEY-1 to R-KEY-3, R-ENC-1, R-ENC-2, R-POT-1,
R-POT-2, R-LED-1 to R-LED-3, R-INPUT-1 to R-INPUT-3).

  fw-suite.py --build DIR --out DIR

Copies DIR/app.bin (a tools/build.sh output) to out/fw/app.bin and builds
the test images (TEST_BUILDS: the same source with one SB_TEST_* define
each) to out/fw/<name>.bin, where tests/fw/boot.suite expects them, runs
the suite through tools/fwtest (the pinned image), and then checks:

- every case: the outcome the suite expects, no unmodelled accesses
  (until M5 also that core 1 never ran: since M5 it runs the FM engine);
- boot: the marker; the vector table, every slot (HW-18): source 4 is
  sb_tick, source 16 lcd_spi_done, source 5 input_scan (since M3), every
  other source its own stub in crt0.S, by the ELF's
  symbols; the clock measured at startup: SB_CLOCK_CYCLES core cycles take
  CLOCK_TICKS time base ticks (240 MHz against 24 MHz, HW-11, HW-13); the
  first tick within FIRST_TICK_MS of the start (from the last tick's time
  base, the ticks taken and the shortest interval, since the run itself
  ends late); nothing halted;
- heartbeat (one emulated second; the image idles between ticks, so
  captures come late, docs/HARNESS.md "Time"): at every capture at least
  one of the beacon's two heartbeat copies is consistent, beats ==
  ticks // 24000, and both are when its seq is even (the tick handler
  writes them in turn, DESIGN-NOTES.md M1); the consistent copy's ticks
  are no earlier than the time asked less one tick period and START_SLACK,
  and no more than LATE_MS after it; beats never go back. At the end:
  the last tick's time base lies within one tick period (and START_SLACK)
  before fwtest's emulated end time; every interval between two ticks is
  within INTERVAL_TOL of 24 000 time base ticks (1 ms), and so is their
  spread (jitter); beats and ticks taken differ by at most one; the idle
  wait returned at least once per tick and (since M3) at most once per
  interrupt, and core 0 ran at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions per tick
  (M0's polling heartbeat: M0_IPP per period);
- fault and stray: the halt recorded in the beacon (reason and source),
  and the console line, by golden file;
- badinsn: fwtest's own fault outcome for an undecodable instruction. A
  limit of the harness, not firmware behaviour: no handler of ours runs
  (SR-1).
- heartbeat2 (since M2): the heartbeat's checks again over 2.25 s; with
  heartbeat (1.25 s) its difference is the steady state, which may take
  at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions a tick. The idle loop's wakes, stored
  once a second, equal the ticks taken since it began, within one.
- screen (since M2): every pixel of the address pattern (300 ms) against
  its formula; the test screen's border, corners and ramps pixel by pixel
  (800 ms); one heartbeat later (1 500 ms) only the heartbeat's rows
  changed; the beacon's screen and seconds shown at each capture; and the
  three pictures against golden images.
- flood (since M2): a test build that sends whole frames back to back from
  500 ms: every tick interval still within INTERVAL_TOL, far more frames
  than ticks, and the picture still the test screen. Prints how long a
  whole frame takes.

- since M3, the panel (tests/fw/scripts/; docs/REQUIREMENTS.md has the
  limits): the input record after the beacon holds the counters, each
  control's value and the last 128 events, each stamped in time base ticks
  from when main started the time base. Each case's events (control, kind,
  value, never times) are compared with tests/fw/events/<case>.txt, and
  written as events.txt beside its outputs. Latencies run from the
  script's time of a change to the event's stamp, allowing for the time

  script): from input_led to the scan first driving that LED, within
  LED_SHOW_MS (one scan).

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Builds everything inside the pinned build container (tools/Dockerfile).
#
#   tools/build.sh image                      build the container image
#   tools/build.sh image-tag                  print its tag
#   tools/build.sh build --out DIR [--src-mount PATH] [--define NAME]...
#                        [--demo plaits]
#                                             build in a fresh container,
#                                             outputs and SHA256SUMS in DIR;
#                                             --define adds -DNAME (test
#                                             builds only, tools/perf.py);
#                                             --demo builds a demo's own
#                                             image instead (M4b: the
#                                             Plaits load test), never the
#                                             firmware's
#   tools/build.sh inside SRC OUT             (runs inside the container)
#
# Builds are deterministic (R-REPRO-3): fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH (set in the
# image), no network, relative source paths with -fdebug-prefix-map, sorted
# output lists, and a check that no output contains the source mount path.
set -eu
ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PLATFORM=linux/amd64
sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
    else shasum -a 256 "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1; fi
}
image_tag() {
    echo "small-beeps-build:$(sha256 "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile" | cut -c1-16)"
}
cmd_image() {
    # No build context: the Dockerfile fetches everything it needs.
    docker build --platform "$PLATFORM" -t "$(image_tag)" - < "$ROOT/tools/Dockerfile"
    docker image inspect --format 'image {{.Id}}' "$(image_tag)"
}
cmd_build() {
    out="" src_mount=/mnt/small-beeps-src defines="" demo=""
    while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
        case "$1" in
            --out) out=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --src-mount) src_mount=$2; shift 2 ;;
            --define)
                case "$2" in
                    ''|*[!A-Z0-9_]*) echo "build: --define takes a NAME of A-Z, 0-9 and _" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                defines="$defines $2"; shift 2 ;;
            --demo)
                case "$2" in
                    plaits) demo=$2 ;;
                    *) echo "build: --demo takes plaits" >&2; exit 2 ;;
                esac
                shift 2 ;;
            *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    [ -n "$out" ] || { echo "build: --out DIR is required" >&2; exit 2; }
    tag=$(image_tag)
    docker image inspect "$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1 || cmd_image
    rm -rf "$out"
    mkdir -p "$out"
    out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)
    docker run --rm --platform "$PLATFORM" --network none \
        --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e SB_DEFINES="$defines" -e SB_DEMO="$demo" \
        -v "$ROOT:$src_mount:ro" -v "$out:/out" -w "$src_mount" \
        "$tag" sh "$src_mount/tools/build.sh" inside "$src_mount" /out
    cat "$out/SHA256SUMS"
}
# The image's size in bytes, from the symbols firmware/app.ld defines:
# code (code and constants, in the image), data (initialised data: in the
# image and copied to RAM), bss (zeroed RAM, the beacon included), image
# (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the top of RAM, both
24:MEMORY
26:    IMAGE (rx)  : ORIGIN = 0x02000000, LENGTH = 0x000FC000
27:    RAM   (rwx) : ORIGIN = 0x01C00000, LENGTH = 0x0007FC00
43:     * beacon, then (since M3) the input record and (since M4) the audio
45:    .beacon (NOLOAD) : {
47:        KEEP(*(.beacon))
48:        KEEP(*(.beacon.input))
49:        KEEP(*(.beacon.audio))
50:        KEEP(*(.beacon.fm))
51:        KEEP(*(.beacon.midi))
70:    __stack_top = ORIGIN(RAM) + LENGTH(RAM);
75:    ASSERT(ADDR(.beacon) == 0x01C00000, "the beacon must start main RAM")

# (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the top of RAM, both
# stacks) and irq_stack (the lower part of it: the interrupt stack).
write_size() {
    sym() { nm "$1" | awk -v s="$2" '$3 == s { print $1 }'; }
    hex() { printf '%d' "0x$1"; }
    origin=$(hex 02000000)
    data_load=$(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_load)")
    data=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_start)") ))
    bss=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_start)") ))
    stack=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    irq=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __irq_stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    printf 'code %d\ndata %d\nbss %d\nimage %d\nstack %d\nirq_stack %d\n' \
        $((data_load - origin)) "$data" "$bss" $((data_load - origin + data)) "$stack" "$irq"
}

# The Plaits demo's own sources and the vendored Plaits (M4b,
# docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md): our C glue and runtime with the firmware's flags;
# our C++ with the same warnings, as errors (Plaits' headers are system
# headers to it: their warnings are not ours to fix); the vendored files
# unmodified at upstream's -O2, with warnings off. All the C++ is built in
# upstream's portable configuration (-DTEST), with our standard headers
# and plaits_pre.h in place of a C library's. Objects are named after their
# paths, since vendored names repeat.
build_demo_plaits() {
    d=firmware/demos/plaits
    CXX="clang -target pi32v2 -x c++ -std=c++11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -fno-exceptions
         -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -fno-common -g -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
         -I$d/include -isystem vendor/plaits/eurorack -isystem vendor/plaits -I$d -Ifirmware/src
         -DTEST -include $d/include/plaits_pre.h"
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXX="$CXX -D$d2"; done
    # PLAITS_HWFLOAT: the toolchain's hardware single-precision float
    # instructions (its fprev1 feature) instead of our soft-float, for the
    # C++ only: a measurement of what they would save, never the demo's
    # default, since whether the chip has them is open (SR-5).
    case " ${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
        *" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*) CXX="$CXX -Xclang -target-feature -Xclang +fprev1" ;;
    esac
    defs=""
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do defs="$defs -D$d2"; done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS $defs -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        set -x; $CXX -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        $CXX -O2 -w -c "$s" -o "$o"
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    echo "built $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | wc -l) vendored Plaits files"
}

cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -DSB_DEMO_PLAITS -Ifirmware/demos/plaits"
    fi
    for s in $(find firmware/src -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        build_demo_plaits
    fi
    set -x
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error -T firmware/app.ld \
        -o "$out/app.elf" $objs
    # The raw image is the code, then the initial data, which app.ld loads
    # right after it. This objcopy takes one section at a time, and ld's
    # own binary output gets data addresses wrong, so the two are joined.
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app.elf" "$obj/text.bin"
    objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app.elf" "$obj/data.bin"
    cat "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin" > "$out/app.bin"
    rm "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin"
    set +x
    write_size "$out/app.elf" > "$out/app.size"
    cat "$out/app.size"
    image=$(awk '$1 == "image" { print $2 }' "$out/app.size")
    if [ "$(wc -c < "$out/app.bin")" -ne "$image" ]; then
        echo "FAIL: app.bin is not the $image bytes app.ld lays out" >&2; exit 1
    fi
    # No output may contain the absolute source path.
    for f in $(find "$out" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        if grep -q -F "$src" "$f"; then
            echo "FAIL: $f contains the source path $src" >&2; exit 1
        fi
    done
    (cd "$out" && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS | sed 's|^\./||' \
        | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS)
}

case "${1:-}" in
    image) cmd_image ;;
    image-tag) image_tag ;;
    build) shift; cmd_build "$@" ;;
    inside) shift; cmd_inside "$@" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,12p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
{

Sizes are bytes: code (code and constants in the image), static_ram (initialised and zeroed data), stack_high_water (the deepest the stack went in the perf runs). Raising a budget, or moving to the next milestone's, takes its own pull request that says why (What/Why/How/Result), with nothing else in it.",
  "milestone": "M6",
  "speed_rise_percent": 3,
  "budgets": {

      "code": 512,
      "static_ram": 64,
      "stack_high_water": 256
    },

# (the raw image's length), stack (reserved at the top of RAM, both
# stacks) and irq_stack (the lower part of it: the interrupt stack).
write_size() {
    sym() { nm "$1" | awk -v s="$2" '$3 == s { print $1 }'; }
    hex() { printf '%d' "0x$1"; }
    origin=$(hex 02000000)
    data_load=$(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_load)")
    data=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __data_start)") ))
    bss=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_end)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __bss_start)") ))
    stack=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    irq=$(( $(hex "$(sym "$1" __irq_stack_top)") - $(hex "$(sym "$1" __stack_limit)") ))
    printf 'code %d\ndata %d\nbss %d\nimage %d\nstack %d\nirq_stack %d\n' \
        $((data_load - origin)) "$data" "$bss" $((data_load - origin + data)) "$stack" "$irq"
}

# The Plaits demo's own sources and the vendored Plaits (M4b,
# docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md): our C glue and runtime with the firmware's flags;
# our C++ with the same warnings, as errors (Plaits' headers are system
# headers to it: their warnings are not ours to fix); the vendored files
# unmodified at upstream's -O2, with warnings off. All the C++ is built in
# upstream's portable configuration (-DTEST), with our standard headers
# and plaits_pre.h in place of a C library's. Objects are named after their
# paths, since vendored names repeat.
build_demo_plaits() {
    d=firmware/demos/plaits
    CXX="clang -target pi32v2 -x c++ -std=c++11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -fno-exceptions
         -fno-rtti -fno-threadsafe-statics -fno-common -g -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
         -I$d/include -isystem vendor/plaits/eurorack -isystem vendor/plaits -I$d -Ifirmware/src
         -DTEST -include $d/include/plaits_pre.h"
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CXX="$CXX -D$d2"; done
    # PLAITS_HWFLOAT: the toolchain's hardware single-precision float
    # instructions (its fprev1 feature) instead of our soft-float, for the
    # C++ only: a measurement of what they would save, never the demo's
    # default, since whether the chip has them is open (SR-5).
    case " ${SB_DEFINES:-} " in
        *" PLAITS_HWFLOAT "*) CXX="$CXX -Xclang -target-feature -Xclang +fprev1" ;;
    esac
    defs=""
    for d2 in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do defs="$defs -D$d2"; done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS $defs -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086,SC2046
            *) set -x; clang $(echo "$CFLAGS" | sed 's/ -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1//') -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find "$d" -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        set -x; $CXX -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    for s in $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(echo "$s" | tr / _ | sed 's/\.cc$/.o/')"
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        $CXX -O2 -w -c "$s" -o "$o"
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    echo "built $(find vendor/plaits -name '*.cc' | wc -l) vendored Plaits files"
}

cmd_inside() {
    src=$1 out=$2
    cd "$src"
    # The chip's CPU model and its single-precision float instructions, as
    # the SDK builds for it (HW-62, since M5). The Plaits demo's own C is
    # built without them, as before (build_demo_plaits): its soft-float
    # test must exercise the soft-float routines, and `-mcpu=r3` on its
    # own already makes the compiler use the instructions.
    CPU="-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1"
    # -nostdinc: no C library headers either; the SDK's register headers
    # are the only outside includes. -fno-common puts zeroed data in .bss.
    CFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -nostdinc -Os -g
            -fno-common -Wall -Wextra -Werror -fdebug-prefix-map=$src=.
            -Ifirmware/src -Ivendor/jieli-sdk/include_lib/driver/cpu/wl82/asm"
    for d in ${SB_DEFINES:-}; do CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -D$d"; done
    # Assembly is built without -g, which would record the source path.
    ASFLAGS="-target pi32v2 $CPU -nostdinc -Werror"
    clang --version | head -1
    ld --version | head -1
    echo "SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH=$SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH"
    # Objects are intermediate: kept out of the outputs.
    obj=/tmp/small-beeps-obj
    rm -rf "$obj" && mkdir -p "$obj"
    objs=""
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        CFLAGS="$CFLAGS -DSB_DEMO_PLAITS -Ifirmware/demos/plaits"
    fi
    for s in $(find firmware/src -name '*.c' -o -name '*.S' | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        o="$obj/$(basename "$s" | sed 's/\.[cS]$/.o/')"
        case "$s" in
            *.S) set -x; clang $ASFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
            # shellcheck disable=SC2086
            *) set -x; clang $CFLAGS -c "$s" -o "$o"; set +x ;;
        esac
        objs="$objs $o"
    done
    if [ -n "${SB_DEMO:-}" ]; then
        build_demo_plaits
    fi
    set -x
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    ld -nostdlib --no-undefined --orphan-handling=error -T firmware/app.ld \
        -o "$out/app.elf" $objs
    # The raw image is the code, then the initial data, which app.ld loads
    # right after it. This objcopy takes one section at a time, and ld's
    # own binary output gets data addresses wrong, so the two are joined.
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/app.elf" "$obj/text.bin"
    objcopy -O binary -j .data "$out/app.elf" "$obj/data.bin"
    cat "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin" > "$out/app.bin"
    rm "$obj/text.bin" "$obj/data.bin"
    set +x
    write_size "$out/app.elf" > "$out/app.size"
    cat "$out/app.size"
    image=$(awk '$1 == "image" { print $2 }' "$out/app.size")
    if [ "$(wc -c < "$out/app.bin")" -ne "$image" ]; then
        echo "FAIL: app.bin is not the $image bytes app.ld lays out" >&2; exit 1
    fi
    # No output may contain the absolute source path.
    for f in $(find "$out" -type f | LC_ALL=C sort); do
        if grep -q -F "$src" "$f"; then
            echo "FAIL: $f contains the source path $src" >&2; exit 1
        fi
    done
    (cd "$out" && find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS | sed 's|^\./||' \
        | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS)
}

case "${1:-}" in
    image) cmd_image ;;
    image-tag) image_tag ;;
    build) shift; cmd_build "$@" ;;
    inside) shift; cmd_inside "$@" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,12p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

/*
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
 * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
 *
 * MIDI out (M6b; docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M6b): a queue of messages, and the
 * transmitter that drains it through UART1's transmit side (HW-72 to
 * HW-74). On the FM-1 the bytes reach no socket (HW-67); in the app they
 * reach other programs.
 *
 * - The engine's block callback (audio.h) is the only writer and the only
 *   reader: midi_out_send() queues a message, midi_out_poll() sends what
 *   waits. Nothing else touches the queue or the UART's transmit side, so
 *   there is no lock and nothing ever waits for the wire.
 * - The transmitter starts a transfer (transmit DMA: TXADR, then TXCNT)
 *   only when the last one has gone (CON0 bit 15, HW-73), never while one
 *   runs, and never changes the bytes of one that runs. A transfer takes
 *   whole messages, up to MIDI_OUT_CHUNK bytes; the poll comes once at
 *   the start of each block and once after the block's events, so a
 *   message queued then has its first byte on the wire at once if the
 *   wire is free.
 * - Running status: a channel message leaves out its status byte when it
 *   is the one sent last, as long as the transmitter has not run dry; the
 *   first message after the queue emptied and the wire went quiet always
 *   carries its status (so a receiver plugged in meanwhile is never left
 *   guessing). System common messages end running status; realtime
 *   messages don't.
 * - When the wire can't keep up (the policy, docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M6b):
 *   a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change replaces a
 *   waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or note), if no
 *   note, mode or other message waits after it; MIDI_OUT_RESERVE places
 *   are kept for note offs (and all notes off, all sound off); any other
 *   message that finds the rest full is dropped and counted, and a note
 *   on dropped so has its note off dropped too, so the far end never
 *   holds a note it was not sent.
 */

#ifndef MIDI_OUT_H
#define MIDI_OUT_H

#include "sb.h"
#include "midi.h"

#define MIDI_OUT_QUEUE   32u   /* messages; at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire */
#define MIDI_OUT_RESERVE 8u    /* of them, kept for note offs */
#define MIDI_OUT_CHUNK   12u   /* the most bytes one transfer takes (3.8 ms) */

/* Queues a message (struct midi_msg, midi.h: a status and 0 to 2 data
 * bytes). Engine callback only. Returns 1 if it was queued or merged with
 * a waiting one, 0 if the policy dropped it. */
int midi_out_send(const struct midi_msg *m);
/* A channel message on the out channel (midi_settings.out_channel). */
int midi_out_channel(u32 kind, u32 d1, u32 d2);
/* Sends what waits, if the wire is free. Engine callback only. */
void midi_out_poll(void);

/* --- The MIDI out record, after MIDI in's (firmware/app.ld) ------------ */
#define MIDI_OUT_MARKER 0x424F444Du   /* "MDOB" in memory order */
struct sb_midi_out_record {
    u32 marker;
    u32 queued;         /* messages queued */
    u32 merged;         /* messages that replaced a waiting one */
    u32 dropped;        /* messages the policy dropped (queue full) */
    u32 offs_dropped;   /* note offs dropped because their note on was */
    u32 offs_lost;      /* note offs dropped with even the reserve full */
    u32 waiting_max;    /* the most messages waiting at once */
    u32 messages;       /* messages handed to the wire */
    u32 bytes;          /* bytes handed to the wire */
    u32 running;        /* status bytes left out (running status) */
    u32 transfers;      /* transfers started */
    u32 busy_starts;    /* transfers started while one ran: always 0 */
    u32 polls_busy;     /* polls that found a transfer still running */
    u32 thru;           /* messages MIDI thru passed on */
    u32 thru_sysex;     /* System Exclusive messages thru did not pass on */
    u32 panel_notes;    /* note ons the panel sent */
    u32 panel_ccs;      /* control changes the panel's knobs sent */
    u32 panel_programs; /* program changes the panel sent */
    u32 last_note_tick; /* sb_ticks() when the panel's last note on was queued */
    u32 last_start_tick;/* sb_ticks() when the last transfer started */
};
extern volatile struct sb_midi_out_record sb_midi_out;

#endif

def bend(v, ch=0):
    return [0xE0 | ch, v & 0x7F, v >> 7]


# --- The cases ---------------------------------------------------------

def midimsg():
    s = Script("midimsg", "midimsg (R-MIDI-2, R-MIDI-3): every message the engine takes, on\n"
               "channel 1, test patch 0 then 8 by program change. Ends with every\n"
               "note off and every voice idle.")
    s.at(100).midi(on(60, 100)).wait(150).midi(off(60))
    s.wait(150).midi(on(62, 90)).wait(150).midi(on(62, 0))          # velocity 0 is an off
    s.wait(150).midi(on(64, 127)).wait(50).midi(bend(16383)).wait(100).midi(bend(0))
    s.wait(100).midi(bend(8192)).wait(50).midi(cc(1, 127)).wait(200).midi(cc(1, 0)).midi(off(64))
    # The bend range by RPN 0: 12 semitones, then a bend to the top.
    s.wait(100).midi(cc(101, 0), cc(100, 0), cc(6, 12), cc(101, 127), cc(100, 127))
    s.wait(50).midi(on(65, 100)).midi(bend(16383)).wait(100).midi(bend(8192)).midi(off(65))
    s.wait(100).midi(cc(7, 64), cc(11, 100)).midi(on(67, 100)).wait(100).midi(off(67))
    s.wait(100).midi(cc(7, 127), cc(11, 127))
    # The knobs' controllers, then back to the middle.
    s.wait(50).midi(cc(16, 127), cc(17, 0), cc(18, 0), cc(19, 127))
    s.wait(50).midi(cc(16, 64), cc(17, 64), cc(18, 64), cc(19, 64))
    # All notes off, all sound off.
    s.wait(100).midi(on(60, 100), on(64, 100), on(67, 100)).wait(100).midi(cc(123, 0))

| `key N tap [HOLD]` | Pressed, then released HOLD ms later (default 50). |

| `midi HH ...` | Bytes (two hex digits each) arrive at the MIDI input one after another, at the wire's pace: one byte every 320 µs, the first 320 µs after the event's time. to the panel and to the key matrix.

"""A reference model of the firmware's MIDI 1.0 byte parser (M6a;
firmware/src/midi.c, docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M6a, "The parser").

Written again from the same rules, not from the C, so the fwtest MIDI
cases can check the firmware's record against it: the messages it logs
(status, data 1, data 2, length) and its counters, for any byte stream.

  midi_model.py HH HH ...      prints the messages and counters

Rules (the MIDI 1.0 specification's):
- 0xF8 to 0xFF are realtime: a message of their own wherever they come,
  even between a status and its data, changing nothing else; 0xF9 and
  0xFD are undefined (counted, dropped); 0xFF, a reset, also clears
  running status and any SysEx.
- 0xF0 starts a System Exclusive message: its data bytes are skipped
  (counted; past SYSEX_LIMIT it is counted as too long). 0xF7 ends it and
  is logged as (0xF0, length & 0x7F, min(length >> 7, 0x7F), 2). Any other
  status but realtime cuts it short (counted).
- Every non-realtime status ends running status. A channel status (0x80
  to 0xEF) starts it: its data bytes follow (one for 0xC0 and 0xD0, two
  for the rest), and further data bytes reuse it. System common: 0xF1 and
  0xF3 take one, 0xF2 two, 0xF6 none; no running status after them. 0xF4
  and 0xF5 are undefined, and an 0xF7 with no SysEx is a stray: counted.
- A status that arrives while a message still waits for its data cuts it
  short (counted). A data byte with no status is an orphan (counted).
"""

import sys

SYSEX_LIMIT = 4096
COUNTERS = ("parsed", "messages", "realtime", "sysex", "sysex_bytes", "sysex_long",
            "sysex_cut", "orphans", "undefined", "cut")


def data_bytes(s):
    if s < 0xF0:
        return 1 if (s & 0xF0) in (0xC0, 0xD0) else 2
    return {0xF1: 1, 0xF3: 1, 0xF2: 2, 0xF6: 0}.get(s)


class Parser:
    def __init__(self):
        self.count = dict.fromkeys(COUNTERS, 0)
        self.log = []
        self.reset()

    def reset(self):
        self.status, self.need, self.data = 0, 0, []
        self.sysex, self.sysex_len = False, 0

    def emit(self, status, d1=0, d2=0, length=0):
        self.log.append((status, d1, d2, length))
        self.count["messages"] += 1

    def end_pending(self):
        if self.sysex:
            self.count["sysex_cut"] += 1
            self.sysex = False
        if self.status and self.data:
            self.count["cut"] += 1
        self.data = []

    def byte(self, b):
        c = self.count
        c["parsed"] += 1
        if b >= 0xF8:
            if b in (0xF9, 0xFD):
                c["undefined"] += 1
                return
            c["realtime"] += 1
            self.emit(b)
            if b == 0xFF:
                self.end_pending()
                self.reset()
            return
        if b >= 0x80:
            ended = False
            if b == 0xF7 and self.sysex:
                n = self.sysex_len
                self.emit(0xF0, n & 0x7F, min(n >> 7, 0x7F), 2)
                self.sysex = False
                ended = True
            else:
                self.end_pending()
            self.status, self.need = 0, 0
            if b == 0xF0:
                self.sysex, self.sysex_len = True, 0
                c["sysex"] += 1
            elif b == 0xF7:
                if not ended:
                    c["undefined"] += 1
            else:
                n = data_bytes(b)
                if n is None:
                    c["undefined"] += 1
                elif n == 0:
                    self.emit(b)
                else:
                    self.status, self.need = b, n
            return
        if self.sysex:
            self.sysex_len += 1
            c["sysex_bytes"] += 1
            if self.sysex_len == SYSEX_LIMIT + 1:
                c["sysex_long"] += 1
            return
        if not self.status:
            c["orphans"] += 1
            return
        self.data.append(b)
        if len(self.data) < self.need:
            return
        d = self.data + [0]
        self.emit(self.status, d[0], d[1] if self.need > 1 else 0, self.need)
        self.data = []
        if self.status >= 0xF0:
            self.status = 0

               "sysex_bytes", "sysex_long", "sysex_cut", "orphans", "undefined", "cut", "filtered",
               "notes_on", "notes_off", "held", "pedal", "bend", "mod", "volume", "expression",

MIDI_MARKER = 0x3649444D      # "MDI6", firmware/src/midi.h
MIDI_LOG = 64
MIDI_LATENCY_MS = 3.0         # a note on's last byte to its first sample (R-MIDI-7)
MIDI_BEND_SEMI = 0.05         # a bent pitch, against the range asked
MIDI_LEVEL_DB = 0.1           # volume and expression against their curve
MIDI_SOUND_OFF_MS = 6.0       # all sound off: silent within this of its last byte


def midi_record(path):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        b = f.read()
    n = len(MIDI_FIELDS)
    r = dict(zip(MIDI_FIELDS, struct.unpack("<%dI" % n, b[:4 * n])))
    r["bend"] = struct.unpack("<i", struct.pack("<I", r["bend"]))[0]
    r["log"] = [tuple(b[4 * n + 4 * i:4 * n + 4 * i + 4]) for i in range(MIDI_LOG)]
    return r


def midi_name(when="end"):
    return "ram-%08x-%x-%s.bin" % (MIDI_ADDR, MIDI_LEN, when)


def midi_logged(r):
    """The messages still in the record's log, oldest first."""
    n = r["log_count"]
    return [r["log"][i % MIDI_LOG] for i in range(max(0, n - MIDI_LOG), n)]


def midi_notes(model, channel=None):
    """(note ons, note offs) the engine should take from the model's log."""
    on = off = 0
    for s, d1, d2, _ in model.log:
        if s >= 0xF0 or (channel is not None and s & 15 != channel):
            continue
        if s & 0xF0 == 0x90 and d2:
            on += 1
        elif s & 0xF0 in (0x80, 0x90):
            off += 1
    return on, off


def midi_common(name, case_dir, idle=True, channel=None):
    """Every MIDI case: fwtest dropped no byte; the firmware received and
    parsed every byte of the script, and its counters and its log of
    messages are the model's (tools/midi_model.py) for the same bytes; it
    took the note ons and offs the model's messages hold; and, if idle,
    nothing is held and no voice sounds at the end."""
    problems, lines = [], []
    with open(os.path.join(case_dir, "result.json")) as f:
        run = json.load(f).get("run", {})
    if run.get("midi_bytes_dropped"):
        problems.append("%s: fwtest dropped %s MIDI bytes" % (name, run["midi_bytes_dropped"]))
    stream = [b for _, b in midi_scripts.stream(os.path.join(ROOT, "tests", "fw", "scripts", name + ".txt"))]
    model = midi_model.parse(stream)
    r = midi_record(os.path.join(case_dir, midi_name()))
    if r["marker"] != MIDI_MARKER:
        return problems + ["%s: the MIDI record's marker is 0x%08x" % (name, r["marker"])], lines, r, model
    if (r["bytes"], r["ring_dropped"], r["parsed"]) != (len(stream), 0, len(stream)):
        problems.append("%s: %d bytes received, %d dropped, %d parsed; the script sends %d"

    for k in midi_model.COUNTERS:
        if r[k] != model.count[k]:

    if r["log_count"] != len(model.log):

    on, off = midi_notes(model, channel)

    """Arrival times (ms) of the last byte of each message in a script

    out, cur, have = [], 0, []
    for t, b in midi_scripts.stream(os.path.join(ROOT, "tests", "fw", "scripts", name + ".txt")):

    r["log"] = [tuple(b[4 * n + 4 * i:4 * n + 4 * i + 4]) for i in range(MIDI_LOG)]
    return r


def midi_name(when="end"):
    return "ram-%08x-%x-%s.bin" % (MIDI_ADDR, MIDI_LEN, when)


def midi_logged(r):
    """The messages still in the record's log, oldest first."""
    n = r["log_count"]
    return [r["log"][i % MIDI_LOG] for i in range(max(0, n - MIDI_LOG), n)]


def midi_notes(model, channel=None):
    """(note ons, note offs) the engine should take from the model's log."""
    on = off = 0
    for s, d1, d2, _ in model.log:
        if s >= 0xF0 or (channel is not None and s & 15 != channel):
            continue
        if s & 0xF0 == 0x90 and d2:
            on += 1
        elif s & 0xF0 in (0x80, 0x90):
            off += 1
    return on, off


def midi_common(name, case_dir, idle=True, channel=None):
    """Every MIDI case: fwtest dropped no byte; the firmware received and
    parsed every byte of the script, and its counters and its log of
    messages are the model's (tools/midi_model.py) for the same bytes; it
    took the note ons and offs the model's messages hold; and, if idle,
    nothing is held and no voice sounds at the end."""
    problems, lines = [], []
    with open(os.path.join(case_dir, "result.json")) as f:
        run = json.load(f).get("run", {})
    if run.get("midi_bytes_dropped"):
        problems.append("%s: fwtest dropped %s MIDI bytes" % (name, run["midi_bytes_dropped"]))
    stream = [b for _, b in midi_scripts.stream(os.path.join(ROOT, "tests", "fw", "scripts", name + ".txt"))]
    model = midi_model.parse(stream)
    r = midi_record(os.path.join(case_dir, midi_name()))
    if r["marker"] != MIDI_MARKER:
        return problems + ["%s: the MIDI record's marker is 0x%08x" % (name, r["marker"])], lines, r, model
    if (r["bytes"], r["ring_dropped"], r["parsed"]) != (len(stream), 0, len(stream)):
        problems.append("%s: %d bytes received, %d dropped, %d parsed; the script sends %d"
                        % (name, r["bytes"], r["ring_dropped"], r["parsed"], len(stream)))
    for k in midi_model.COUNTERS:
        if r[k] != model.count[k]:
            problems.append("%s: %s %d, the model says %d" % (name, k, r[k], model.count[k]))
    if r["log_count"] != len(model.log):
        problems.append("%s: %d messages logged, the model has %d" % (name, r["log_count"], len(model.log)))
    elif midi_logged(r) != model.log[-MIDI_LOG:]:
        problems.append("%s: the logged messages differ from the model's" % name)
    on, off = midi_notes(model, channel)
    if (r["notes_on"], r["notes_off"]) != (on, off):
        problems.append("%s: %d note ons and %d offs taken, expected %d and %d"
                        % (name, r["notes_on"], r["notes_off"], on, off))
    f = fm_record(os.path.join(case_dir, fm_name()))
    if idle and (r["held"] or r["pedal"] or f["voices0"] or f["voices1"]):
        problems.append("%s: at the end %d notes held, pedal %d, %d + %d voices sounding: a stuck note"
                        % (name, r["held"], r["pedal"], f["voices0"], f["voices1"]))
    lines.append("  midi: %d bytes, %d messages (%d realtime), %d SysEx (%d bytes, %d too long, %d cut), "
                 "%d orphans, %d undefined, %d cut, %d filtered; %d note ons, %d offs; model: same"
                 % (r["bytes"], r["messages"], r["realtime"], r["sysex"], r["sysex_bytes"], r["sysex_long"],
                    r["sysex_cut"], r["orphans"], r["undefined"], r["cut"], r["filtered"],
                    r["notes_on"], r["notes_off"]) if not problems else
                 "  midi: %d bytes, %d messages" % (r["bytes"], r["messages"]))
    return problems, lines, r, model


def midi_times(name, status, d1=None):
    """Arrival times (ms) of the last byte of each message in a script
    whose status (high nibble for channel messages) and first data byte
    match, running status included."""
    out, cur, have = [], 0, []
    for t, b in midi_scripts.stream(os.path.join(ROOT, "tests", "fw", "scripts", name + ".txt")):
        if b >= 0xF8:
            continue
        if b >= 0x80:
            cur, have = (b if b < 0xF0 else 0), []
            continue
        if not cur:
            continue
        have.append(b)
        if len(have) == midi_model.data_bytes(cur):
            if (cur & 0xF0) == status and (d1 is None or have[0] == d1):
                out.append((t, have))
            have = []
    return out


def pitch_at(x, ends, t0, t1):
    """The median pitch (MIDI note) of the sound between t0 and t1 ms."""
    first = next(i for i in range(len(x)) if aa.sample_ms(i, ends) >= t0)
    last = next(i for i in range(first, len(x)) if aa.sample_ms(i, ends) >= t1)
    track = sorted(69 + 12 * math.log2(hz / 440.0) for _, hz in aa.pitch_track(x, first, last))
    return track[len(track) // 2] if track else None, track


def level_at(x, ends, t0, t1):
    at = lambda ms: next(i for i in range(len(x)) if aa.sample_ms(i, ends) >= ms)
    return rms_db(x[at(t0):at(t1)])

def check_midilat(case_dir):
    """Latency (R-MIDI-7): from each note on's last byte (the script's time
    and the wire's pace, docs/HARNESS.md) to the first sample of its sound
    (ipb.csv's block ends, exact), within MIDI_LATENCY_MS."""
    problems, lines, a, _, wav = check_audio_common("midilat", case_dir)
    more, l2, r, _ = midi_common("midilat", case_dir)
    problems, lines = problems + more, lines + l2
    if wav is None:
        return problems + ["midilat: no audio.wav"], lines
    x, ends = wav
    starts = [aa.sample_ms(first, ends) for first, _ in sounds(x)]
    ons = [t for t, d in midi_times("midilat", 0x90) if d[1]]
    lat = []
    for t in ons:
        s = [u for u in starts if u >= t]
        lat.append(s[0] - t if s else None)
    if len(starts) != len(ons) or None in lat:
        return problems + ["midilat: %d sounds for %d note ons" % (len(starts), len(ons))], lines

                 % (min(lat), max(lat), sum(lat) / len(lat), MIDI_LATENCY_MS, len(lat)))
    if max(lat) > MIDI_LATENCY_MS or min(lat) < 0:

content.content:
## Golden files

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

## Suites

`fwtest suite FILE --out DIR` runs several cases. Each line of FILE:

```
# NAME  EXPECT     IMAGE                 run options (paths relative to FILE)
boot    completed  ../out/build/app.bin  --ms 50 --ram 0x01c00000:16@end --golden golden/boot
stop    halt       images/stop.bin       --ms 10
```

NAME (letters, digits, `-`, `_`) is the case's output folder under DIR.
EXPECT is the outcome expected: `completed`, `halt`, `fault` or `hang`. A
case passes when its outcome is EXPECT and every golden file matches. DIR
also gets `result.json` (every case's result) and `junit.xml` (one test case
per suite case). The exit code is 0 when every case passes, 1 otherwise, 2
on a usage error.

## Determinism

The same image, script, options and fwtest build give byte-identical outputs
on every run and every machine: no host time, no randomness that isn't
seeded the same way every run, nothing from the environment, no host paths
in the results. CI runs the harness's own suite twice in fresh containers
and compares every output byte (C-HARNESS-DET). If two runs of yours ever
