entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

cat >> docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md <<'EOF'

### 2026-10-24 M6b: MIDI out
- Facts: HW-72 to HW-74 (the SMK-37's MIDI OUT is a UART's transmit side;
  UART1 transmits by DMA, `TXADR` then `TXCNT`, and sets `CON0` bit 15
  when the last byte has gone, cleared by writing bit 13; the FM-1 has no
  MIDI OUT jack, so its bytes reach no socket); HARNESS.md's "MIDI
  output" (`--midi-out`, a byte every 320 us). PROVENANCE P-47, and P-43
  (the MIDI 1.0 specification) for the wire format, running status and
  local control.
- Sources: as M6a's; no other synthesizer's firmware and no MIDI
  library's source was looked at.

#### The path
One context does everything: the engine's block callback. It polls the
transmitter at the start of its events, takes the panel's events (and
queues what they send), takes MIDI in (and queues what thru passes on),
then polls again, so a message queued in a block has its first byte on
the wire in that block if the wire is free. Nothing else writes the
queue or the UART's transmit side, so there is no lock, and nothing ever
waits for the wire: a poll that finds a transfer still running returns.

#### The transmitter
A poll sends only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15,
acknowledged with bit 13, every write keeping the UART and the receive
DMA on), never while one runs, and a running transfer's 16-byte buffer
is never touched. A transfer takes whole messages, up to 12 bytes (3.8
ms), so under a long stream a new message waits at most that plus a
block. No interrupt: the transmit interrupt's enable bit is known only
from the emulator (HW-74), the receive side is polled the same way
(M6a), and the polls a block gives are enough: the chunk lets the wire
stay busy across a block. Polling costs throughput, though: a transfer
can only start at a poll, so the wire idles from a transfer's end to
the next poll; under a stream the wire carries about 85 to 95% of its
31 250 baud (midiburst's figure below). A full input wire passed on by
thru therefore builds the queue up slowly, and the policy (below)
applies. On the chip, what writing `CON0` during a transfer does beyond
the acknowledge, and whether a pin carries UART1's transmit side at all,
are open (Q-20); nothing here depends on the pin.

#### Running status
A channel message leaves out its status byte when it is the status sent
last, while messages keep coming; when a poll finds the transfer done and
nothing waiting, the wire has gone quiet and the next message carries its
status, so a receiver connected meanwhile is never left without one.
System common messages end running status, realtime messages don't. The
panel's note offs are note ons at velocity 0 (the receiver treats both
the same, M6a), so a run of notes keeps one status.

#### The policy when the wire can't keep up
The queue holds 32 messages (at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire):
- **Merging:** a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change
  replaces a waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or
  note), looking back from the newest over such messages only, so no
  value moves past a note, a mode message or a parameter-number sequence.
  Data entry (6, 38), the parameter numbers (96 to 101) and the mode
  messages (120 to 127) never merge: their order is their meaning.
- **The reserve:** 8 places are kept for note offs (and all notes off,
  all sound off). Any other message that finds the other 24 full is
  dropped and counted.
- **Never a stuck note:** a note on dropped marks its note, and its note
  off is dropped too. A note off that finds all 32 full drops the newest
  waiting message that ends no notes (a note on so dropped marks its
  note). Only a queue of 32 note offs alone could lose one; it is counted.

#### What the panel sends
On the out channel (1 by default):
- **Keys:** a note on at velocity 100 (the keys have no velocity) and a
  note on at velocity 0 when let go, for the note the key started, so an
  octave change while it is held can't leave it on. OCT- and OCT+ only
  move the notes sent.
- **KNOB1 to KNOB4:** as the first controllers M6a's map routes to them
  (16 to 19 by default; a changed map changes them), each value the
  inverse of how MIDI in reads it: the value nearest 64 whose offset is
  the panel knob's position, held to the knob's span. So a far end with
  its own knob at rest takes the position the panel's knob has; a value
  is sent only when it changes. tools/midi_model.py checks every
  position.
- **PRESETS:** a program change, the test patch's number.
- **SEL with MONO or POLY:** the mode messages 126 (value 1) and 127,
  which MIDI in takes as mono and poly.
- **Pitch:** the panel has no bend or pitch wheel; KNOB1 transposes and
  goes as its controller (a bend could not carry ±24 semitones at the
  default range of 2). Not sent: MASTER (the device's own output level,
  not in the map), ALGORITHM (no controller in the map yet; M8), PLAY's
  test tone, SELECT.

#### Thru and local control
- **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message MIDI in parsed, on
  every channel, before the receive channel's filter, realtime and system
  common included, as messages merged with the panel's at message
  boundaries (never bytes, which would break running status). A SysEx is
  not passed on: the parser keeps none of its bytes (M6a); it is counted.
  Only bytes received at MIDI in go through thru, never the firmware's
  own messages. A cable from out to in with thru on would repeat
  messages without end, as on any instrument with soft thru.
- **Local control** (on by default; CC 122 sets it from MIDI, as the
  specification has it): off, the panel's keys, knobs and PRESETS go to
  MIDI out only. The engine keeps the knob positions it last took and
  its patch, and a key let go still ends its note if it had started one
  before. MIDI in still plays, so a sequencer can play the engine from
  the panel's own notes. On again, the engine takes the panel's knobs
  where they are.

#### The settings and the screen
`struct midi_settings` (version 2) adds the out channel (1 to 16), thru
and local control after M6a's fields, all bytes, for M7 to save. The
thru test build sets thru on and the out channel to 2. The panel
screen's bottom line shows them ("MIDI out ch 1  thru off  local on"),
redrawn when they change.
EOF
echo ok

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/PLAN.md'; s=open(p).read()
old='''### M1 to M9 (firmware side)'''
new='''### M6b: MIDI out (firmware side)
- Status 2026-10-24 (session M6b, firmware side, on the owner's Mac): done,
  in pull requests #90 (start) and the MIDI out pull request (the sender,
  what the panel sends, thru, local control, the settings on the screen,
  the tests), which needs fwtest 0.5.0's pin (#91) on main first.
  - **The sender** (HW-72 to HW-74): a 32-message queue that only the
    engine's block callback writes and drains; UART1's transmit DMA,
    started only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15), whole
    messages up to 12 bytes a transfer; no interrupt, no lock, nothing
    waits for the wire. Running status while messages keep coming; the
    first message after the wire goes quiet carries its status.
  - **The policy:** controllers, bends, pressure and program changes merge
    with a waiting one; 8 places kept for note offs; others dropped and
    counted when full; a note on dropped takes its note off with it; a
    note off that finds the queue full drops the newest message that ends
    no notes. Nothing is left on at the far end.
  - **What is sent**, on the out channel (1): the keys (velocity 100, the
    off as velocity 0), KNOB1 to KNOB4 as controllers 16 to 19 (the
    inverse of M6a's map, when the value changes), PRESETS as program
    changes, SEL with MONO or POLY as the mode messages. The panel has no
    other pitch control.
  - **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message received but SysEx,
    before the channel filter; **local control** (on by default, CC 122
    too) off sends the panel to MIDI out only. The settings are in
    `struct midi_settings` version 2 and on the screen's bottom line.
  - **Tests** (fwtest 0.5.0, `--midi-out`): six cases, R-MIDIOUT-1 to
    R-MIDIOUT-8. midiout's 60 messages exactly as its script implies
    (golden); the round trip (midiout's golden capture into MIDI in) ends
    with the same patch, mode and knobs and the same pitches; thru passes
    on 18 messages in order and the panel's 4 once each (golden); local
    control off plays nothing from the panel (golden screen); a burst of
    94 messages in one block: 28 merged, 18 dropped with 16 note offs, none
    lost, every note sent ended, the panel's keys out again after (golden);
    the wire's timing and one run per transfer in every case.
  - **Figures** (fwtest 0.5.0): latency from a key going down to its note
    on's first start bit 3.26 to 5.29 ms (mean 4.20; debounce, then at most
    a block); the wire carries about 88% of its rate under a stream (a
    transfer starts only at a poll). At rest 1 863.9 instructions a block,
    +25 (+1.4%); loaded 110 207.6, +0.3%; code 20 144 bytes (+1 736),
    static RAM 143 776 (+520): the M6 budgets hold, none raised. audiogold
    and fmgold unchanged; chords' and midipanel's screens moved only by
    the settings line.
  - **Open items:**
    - **The transmitter on the chip.** Which pin, if any, carries UART1's
      transmit side on the FM-1 is open (Q-20); the FM-1 has no MIDI OUT
      jack, so on the device the bytes go nowhere; in the app they reach
      other programs. What a `CON0` write during a transfer does on the
      chip, beyond the acknowledge, is not known.
    - **Throughput:** with polling once or twice a block, a full input
      wire passed on by thru is about 12% more than the out wire carries;

# Updated by a pull request after each harness change is published
# (.github/workflows/fwtest-image.yml prints the digest).

against 85 755 without MIDI (a wire filled to the last byte took 116 420
in a one-off run). The M6 budgets (their own pull request) raise the
loaded budget to 131 072 for it; the rest is M5's.
-- Facts: HW-72 to HW-74 (the SMK-37's MIDI OUT is a UART's transmit side;
-  UART1 transmits by DMA, `TXADR` then `TXCNT`, and sets `CON0` bit 15
-  when the last byte has gone, cleared by writing bit 13; the FM-1 has no
-  MIDI OUT jack, so its bytes reach no socket); HARNESS.md's "MIDI
-  output" (`--midi-out`, a byte every 320 us). PROVENANCE P-50, and P-43
-  (the MIDI 1.0 specification) for the wire format, running status and
-  local control.
-- Sources: as M6a's; no other synthesizer's firmware and no MIDI
-  library's source was looked at.
-#### The path
-One context does everything: the engine's block callback. It polls the
-transmitter at the start of its events, takes the panel's events (and
-queues what they send), takes MIDI in (and queues what thru passes on),
-then polls again, so a message queued in a block has its first byte on
-the wire in that block if the wire is free. Nothing else writes the
-queue or the UART's transmit side, so there is no lock, and nothing ever
-waits for the wire: a poll that finds a transfer still running returns.
-#### The transmitter
-A poll sends only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15,
-acknowledged with bit 13, every write keeping the UART and the receive
-DMA on), never while one runs, and a running transfer's 16-byte buffer
-is never touched. A transfer takes whole messages, up to 12 bytes (3.8
-ms), so under a long stream a new message waits at most that plus a
-block. No interrupt: the transmit interrupt's enable bit is known only
-from the emulator (HW-74), the receive side is polled the same way
-(M6a), and the polls a block gives are enough: the chunk lets the wire
-stay busy across a block. Polling costs throughput, though: a transfer
-can only start at a poll, so the wire idles from a transfer's end to
-the next poll; under a stream the wire carries about 88% of its 31 250
-baud (midiburst: 65 bytes in 23.6 ms). A full input wire passed on by
-thru therefore builds the queue up slowly, and the policy (below)
-applies. On the chip, what writing `CON0` during a transfer does beyond
-the acknowledge, and whether a pin carries UART1's transmit side at all,
-are open (Q-20); nothing here depends on the pin.
-#### Running status
-A channel message leaves out its status byte when it is the status sent
-last, while messages keep coming; when a poll finds the transfer done and
-nothing waiting, the wire has gone quiet and the next message carries its
-status, so a receiver connected meanwhile is never left without one.
-System common messages end running status, realtime messages don't. The
-panel's note offs are note ons at velocity 0 (the receiver treats both
-the same, M6a), so a run of notes keeps one status.
-#### The policy when the wire can't keep up
-The queue holds 32 messages (at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire):
-- **Merging:** a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change
-  replaces a waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or
-  note), looking back from the newest over such messages only, so no
-  value moves past a note, a mode message or a parameter-number sequence.
-  Data entry (6, 38), the parameter numbers (96 to 101) and the mode
-  messages (120 to 127) never merge: their order is their meaning.
-- **The reserve:** 8 places are kept for note offs (and all notes off,
-  all sound off). Any other message that finds the other 24 full is
-  dropped and counted.
-- **Never a stuck note:** a note on dropped marks its note, and its note
-  off is dropped too. A note off that finds all 32 full drops the newest
-  waiting message that ends no notes (a note on so dropped marks its
-  note). Only a queue of 32 note offs alone could lose one; it is counted.
-#### What the panel sends
-On the out channel (1 by default):
-- **Keys:** a note on at velocity 100 (the keys have no velocity) and a
-  note on at velocity 0 when let go, for the note the key started, so an
-  octave change while it is held can't leave it on. OCT- and OCT+ only
-  move the notes sent.
-- **KNOB1 to KNOB4:** as the first controllers M6a's map routes to them
-  (16 to 19 by default; a changed map changes them), each value the
-  inverse of how MIDI in reads it: the value nearest 64 whose offset is
-  the panel knob's position, held to the knob's span. So a far end with
-  its own knob at rest takes the position the panel's knob has; a value
-  is sent only when it changes. tools/midi_model.py checks every
-  position.
-- **PRESETS:** a program change, the test patch's number.
-- **SEL with MONO or POLY:** the mode messages 126 (value 1) and 127,
-  which MIDI in takes as mono and poly.
-- **Pitch:** the panel has no bend or pitch wheel; KNOB1 transposes and
-  goes as its controller (a bend could not carry ±24 semitones at the
-  default range of 2). Not sent: MASTER (the device's own output level,
-  not in the map), ALGORITHM (no controller in the map yet; M8), PLAY's
-  test tone, SELECT.
-#### Thru and local control
-- **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message MIDI in parsed, on
-  every channel, before the receive channel's filter, realtime and system
-  common included, as messages merged with the panel's at message
-  boundaries (never bytes, which would break running status). A SysEx is
-  not passed on: the parser keeps none of its bytes (M6a); it is counted.
-  Only bytes received at MIDI in go through thru, never the firmware's
-  own messages. A cable from out to in with thru on would repeat
-  messages without end, as on any instrument with soft thru.
-- **Local control** (on by default; CC 122 sets it from MIDI, as the
-  specification has it): off, the panel's keys, knobs and PRESETS go to
-  MIDI out only. The engine keeps the knob positions it last took and
-  its patch, and a key let go still ends its note if it had started one
-  before. MIDI in still plays, so a sequencer can play the engine from
-  the panel's own notes. On again, the engine takes the panel's knobs
-  where they are.
-#### The settings and the screen
-`struct midi_settings` (version 2) adds the out channel (1 to 16), thru
-and local control after M6a's fields, all bytes, for M7 to save. The
-thru test build sets thru on and the out channel to 2. The panel
-screen's bottom line shows them ("MIDI out ch 1  thru off  local on"),
-redrawn when they change.
-#### Figures (fwtest 0.5.0, through `FWTEST_IMAGE` before its pin)
-- **Latency** from a key going down to its note on's first start bit, 20
-  keys: 3.260 to 5.286 ms, mean 4.196: the key's debounce (2.5 to 4.5 ms,
-  M3), then up to a block until the engine takes the event; the byte
-  starts in that block.
-- **The burst** (94 messages in one block): 28 merged, 18 dropped (the 10
-  note ons past the room, 6 more and the controller and bend to make room
-  for note offs), 16 note offs dropped with their note ons, none lost; 16
-  notes sent and each ended, 77 bytes in 10 transfers, 31 status bytes
-  left out.
-- **Cost at rest:** 1 863.9 instructions a block, 25 more than M6a's (the
-  two polls of an empty queue); loaded 110 207.6, +0.3% (the perf input's
-  keys and knobs now also go out). Code 20 144 bytes (+1 736), static RAM
-  143 776 (+520: the queue, the transfer buffer, the dropped-note bits,
-  the record).
-- **Never disturbs audio:** no underrun in any case, audiogold and fmgold
-  byte for byte as before.

+- Facts: HW-72 to HW-74 (the SMK-37's MIDI OUT is a UART's transmit side;
+  UART1 transmits by DMA, `TXADR` then `TXCNT`, and sets `CON0` bit 15
+  when the last byte has gone, cleared by writing bit 13; the FM-1 has no
+  MIDI OUT jack, so its bytes reach no socket); HARNESS.md's "MIDI
+  output" (`--midi-out`, a byte every 320 us). PROVENANCE P-50, and P-43
+  (the MIDI 1.0 specification) for the wire format, running status and
+  local control.
+- Sources: as M6a's; no other synthesizer's firmware and no MIDI
+  library's source was looked at.
+#### The path
+One context does everything: the engine's block callback. It polls the
+transmitter at the start of its events, takes the panel's events (and
+queues what they send), takes MIDI in (and queues what thru passes on),
+then polls again, so a message queued in a block has its first byte on
+the wire in that block if the wire is free. Nothing else writes the
+queue or the UART's transmit side, so there is no lock, and nothing ever
+waits for the wire: a poll that finds a transfer still running returns.
+#### The transmitter
+A poll sends only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15,
+acknowledged with bit 13, every write keeping the UART and the receive
+DMA on), never while one runs, and a running transfer's 16-byte buffer
+is never touched. A transfer takes whole messages, up to 12 bytes (3.8
+ms), so under a long stream a new message waits at most that plus a
+block. No interrupt: the transmit interrupt's enable bit is known only
+from the emulator (HW-74), the receive side is polled the same way
+(M6a), and the polls a block gives are enough: the chunk lets the wire
+stay busy across a block. Polling costs throughput, though: a transfer
+can only start at a poll, so the wire idles from a transfer's end to
+the next poll; under a stream the wire carries about 88% of its 31 250
+baud (midiburst: 65 bytes in 23.6 ms). A full input wire passed on by
+thru therefore builds the queue up slowly, and the policy (below)
+applies. On the chip, what writing `CON0` during a transfer does beyond
+the acknowledge, and whether a pin carries UART1's transmit side at all,
+are open (Q-20); nothing here depends on the pin.
+#### Running status
+A channel message leaves out its status byte when it is the status sent
+last, while messages keep coming; when a poll finds the transfer done and
+nothing waiting, the wire has gone quiet and the next message carries its
+status, so a receiver connected meanwhile is never left without one.
+System common messages end running status, realtime messages don't. The
+panel's note offs are note ons at velocity 0 (the receiver treats both
+the same, M6a), so a run of notes keeps one status.
+#### The policy when the wire can't keep up
+The queue holds 32 messages (at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire):
+- **Merging:** a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change
+  replaces a waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or
+  note), looking back from the newest over such messages only, so no
+  value moves past a note, a mode message or a parameter-number sequence.
+  Data entry (6, 38), the parameter numbers (96 to 101) and the mode
+  messages (120 to 127) never merge: their order is their meaning.
+- **The reserve:** 8 places are kept for note offs (and all notes off,
+  all sound off). Any other message that finds the other 24 full is
+  dropped and counted.
+- **Never a stuck note:** a note on dropped marks its note, and its note
+  off is dropped too. A note off that finds all 32 full drops the newest
+  waiting message that ends no notes (a note on so dropped marks its
+  note). Only a queue of 32 note offs alone could lose one; it is counted.
+#### What the panel sends
+On the out channel (1 by default):
+- **Keys:** a note on at velocity 100 (the keys have no velocity) and a
+  note on at velocity 0 when let go, for the note the key started, so an
+  octave change while it is held can't leave it on. OCT- and OCT+ only
+  move the notes sent.
+- **KNOB1 to KNOB4:** as the first controllers M6a's map routes to them
+  (16 to 19 by default; a changed map changes them), each value the
+  inverse of how MIDI in reads it: the value nearest 64 whose offset is
+  the panel knob's position, held to the knob's span. So a far end with
+  its own knob at rest takes the position the panel's knob has; a value
+  is sent only when it changes. tools/midi_model.py checks every
+  position.
+- **PRESETS:** a program change, the test patch's number.
+- **SEL with MONO or POLY:** the mode messages 126 (value 1) and 127,
+  which MIDI in takes as mono and poly.
+- **Pitch:** the panel has no bend or pitch wheel; KNOB1 transposes and
+  goes as its controller (a bend could not carry ±24 semitones at the
+  default range of 2). Not sent: MASTER (the device's own output level,
+  not in the map), ALGORITHM (no controller in the map yet; M8), PLAY's
+  test tone, SELECT.
+#### Thru and local control
+- **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message MIDI in parsed, on
+  every channel, before the receive channel's filter, realtime and system
+  common included, as messages merged with the panel's at message
+  boundaries (never bytes, which would break running status). A SysEx is
+  not passed on: the parser keeps none of its bytes (M6a); it is counted.
+  Only bytes received at MIDI in go through thru, never the firmware's
+  own messages. A cable from out to in with thru on would repeat
+  messages without end, as on any instrument with soft thru.
+- **Local control** (on by default; CC 122 sets it from MIDI, as the
+  specification has it): off, the panel's keys, knobs and PRESETS go to
+  MIDI out only. The engine keeps the knob positions it last took and
+  its patch, and a key let go still ends its note if it had started one
+  before. MIDI in still plays, so a sequencer can play the engine from
+  the panel's own notes. On again, the engine takes the panel's knobs
+  where they are.
+#### The settings and the screen
+`struct midi_settings` (version 2) adds the out channel (1 to 16), thru
+and local control after M6a's fields, all bytes, for M7 to save. The
+thru test build sets thru on and the out channel to 2. The panel
+screen's bottom line shows them ("MIDI out ch 1  thru off  local on"),
+redrawn when they change.
+#### Figures (fwtest 0.5.0, through `FWTEST_IMAGE` before its pin)
+- **Latency** from a key going down to its note on's first start bit, 20
+  keys: 3.260 to 5.286 ms, mean 4.196: the key's debounce (2.5 to 4.5 ms,
+  M3), then up to a block until the engine takes the event; the byte
+  starts in that block.
+- **The burst** (94 messages in one block): 28 merged, 18 dropped (the 10
+  note ons past the room, 6 more and the controller and bend to make room
+  for note offs), 16 note offs dropped with their note ons, none lost; 16
+  notes sent and each ended, 77 bytes in 10 transfers, 31 status bytes
+  left out.
+- **Cost at rest:** 1 863.9 instructions a block, 25 more than M6a's (the
+  two polls of an empty queue); loaded 110 207.6, +0.3% (the perf input's
+  keys and knobs now also go out). Code 20 144 bytes (+1 736), static RAM
+  143 776 (+520: the queue, the transfer buffer, the dropped-note bits,
+  the record).
+- **Never disturbs audio:** no underrun in any case, audiogold and fmgold
+  byte for byte as before.

+    no notes. Nothing is left on at the far end.

+    off as velocity 0), KNOB1 to KNOB4 as controllers 16 to 19 (the
+    inverse of M6a's map, when the value changes), PRESETS as program
+    changes, SEL with MONO or POLY as the mode messages. The panel has no
+    other pitch control.

+    before the channel filter; **local control** (on by default, CC 122
+    too) off sends the panel to MIDI out only. The settings are in
+    `struct midi_settings` version 2 and on the screen's bottom line.

**What:** M6b, MIDI out. `firmware/src/midi_out.c`/`.h`: a 32-message queue and its policy, running status, and the transmitter (UART1's transmit DMA, HW-72 to HW-74). The panel sends its keys, KNOB1 to KNOB4 (controllers 16 to 19, the inverse of M6a's map), PRESETS (program change) and SEL+MONO/POLY (mode messages) on the out channel. Soft thru (off by default) passes on MIDI in's messages. Local control (on by default; CC 122 too) off sends the panel to MIDI out only. The settings (`struct midi_settings` v2) are shown on the panel screen's bottom line. Also six fwtest cases with `--midi-out` and goldens, R-MIDIOUT-1 to R-MIDIOUT-8, the design notes, P-50, and PLAN.md (M6b done, M7 next).

Stacked on #90 (merge it first). No `REVIEWED.json` entries in this PR (#90 lists its five).

**Why:** M6b (R-MIDIOUT-1 to R-MIDIOUT-8).

**How:**
- The engine's block callback is the only writer and reader, so there's no lock and nothing ever waits for the wire.
- It polls `CON0` bit 15 at the start of its events and after them. A transfer (whole messages, up to 12 bytes) starts only when the last one has gone, and its buffer isn't touched while it runs. No transmit interrupt: its enable bit is known only from the emulator.
- Messages are queued, not bytes. Running status is decided when a transfer is filled, and it resets when the wire goes quiet.
- Policy: controllers, bends, pressure and program changes merge with a waiting one of the same kind. 8 places are reserved for note offs. Anything else is dropped and counted when the queue is full. A dropped note on drops its note off too. A note off that finds the queue full evicts the newest message that ends no notes.

-- Facts: HW-72 to HW-74 (the SMK-37's MIDI OUT is a UART's transmit side;
-  UART1 transmits by DMA, `TXADR` then `TXCNT`, and sets `CON0` bit 15
-  when the last byte has gone, cleared by writing bit 13; the FM-1 has no
-  MIDI OUT jack, so its bytes reach no socket); HARNESS.md's "MIDI
-  output" (`--midi-out`, a byte every 320 us). PROVENANCE P-50, and P-43
-  (the MIDI 1.0 specification) for the wire format, running status and
-  local control.
-- Sources: as M6a's; no other synthesizer's firmware and no MIDI
-  library's source was looked at.
-#### The path
-One context does everything: the engine's block callback. It polls the
-transmitter at the start of its events, takes the panel's events (and
-queues what they send), takes MIDI in (and queues what thru passes on),
-then polls again, so a message queued in a block has its first byte on
-the wire in that block if the wire is free. Nothing else writes the
-queue or the UART's transmit side, so there is no lock, and nothing ever
-waits for the wire: a poll that finds a transfer still running returns.
-#### The transmitter
-A poll sends only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15,
-acknowledged with bit 13, every write keeping the UART and the receive
-DMA on), never while one runs, and a running transfer's 16-byte buffer
-is never touched. A transfer takes whole messages, up to 12 bytes (3.8
-ms), so under a long stream a new message waits at most that plus a
-block. No interrupt: the transmit interrupt's enable bit is known only
-from the emulator (HW-74), the receive side is polled the same way
-(M6a), and the polls a block gives are enough: the chunk lets the wire
-stay busy across a block. Polling costs throughput, though: a transfer
-can only start at a poll, so the wire idles from a transfer's end to
-the next poll; under a stream the wire carries about 88% of its 31 250
-baud (midiburst: 65 bytes in 23.6 ms). A full input wire passed on by
-thru therefore builds the queue up slowly, and the policy (below)
-applies. On the chip, what writing `CON0` during a transfer does beyond
-the acknowledge, and whether a pin carries UART1's transmit side at all,
-are open (Q-20); nothing here depends on the pin.
-#### Running status
-A channel message leaves out its status byte when it is the status sent
-last, while messages keep coming; when a poll finds the transfer done and
-nothing waiting, the wire has gone quiet and the next message carries its
-status, so a receiver connected meanwhile is never left without one.
-System common messages end running status, realtime messages don't. The
-panel's note offs are note ons at velocity 0 (the receiver treats both
-the same, M6a), so a run of notes keeps one status.
-#### The policy when the wire can't keep up
-The queue holds 32 messages (at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire):
-- **Merging:** a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change
-  replaces a waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or
-  note), looking back from the newest over such messages only, so no
-  value moves past a note, a mode message or a parameter-number sequence.
-  Data entry (6, 38), the parameter numbers (96 to 101) and the mode
-  messages (120 to 127) never merge: their order is their meaning.
-- **The reserve:** 8 places are kept for note offs (and all notes off,
-  all sound off). Any other message that finds the other 24 full is
-  dropped and counted.
-- **Never a stuck note:** a note on dropped marks its note, and its note
-  off is dropped too. A note off that finds all 32 full drops the newest
-  waiting message that ends no notes (a note on so dropped marks its
-  note). Only a queue of 32 note offs alone could lose one; it is counted.
-#### What the panel sends
-On the out channel (1 by default):
-- **Keys:** a note on at velocity 100 (the keys have no velocity) and a
-  note on at velocity 0 when let go, for the note the key started, so an
-  octave change while it is held can't leave it on. OCT- and OCT+ only
-  move the notes sent.
-- **KNOB1 to KNOB4:** as the first controllers M6a's map routes to them
-  (16 to 19 by default; a changed map changes them), each value the
-  inverse of how MIDI in reads it: the value nearest 64 whose offset is
-  the panel knob's position, held to the knob's span. So a far end with
-  its own knob at rest takes the position the panel's knob has; a value
-  is sent only when it changes. tools/midi_model.py checks every
-  position.
-- **PRESETS:** a program change, the test patch's number.
-- **SEL with MONO or POLY:** the mode messages 126 (value 1) and 127,
-  which MIDI in takes as mono and poly.
-- **Pitch:** the panel has no bend or pitch wheel; KNOB1 transposes and
-  goes as its controller (a bend could not carry ±24 semitones at the
-  default range of 2). Not sent: MASTER (the device's own output level,
-  not in the map), ALGORITHM (no controller in the map yet; M8), PLAY's
-  test tone, SELECT.
-#### Thru and local control
-- **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message MIDI in parsed, on
-  every channel, before the receive channel's filter, realtime and system
-  common included, as messages merged with the panel's at message
-  boundaries (never bytes, which would break running status). A SysEx is
-  not passed on: the parser keeps none of its bytes (M6a); it is counted.
-  Only bytes received at MIDI in go through thru, never the firmware's
-  own messages. A cable from out to in with thru on would repeat
-  messages without end, as on any instrument with soft thru.
-- **Local control** (on by default; CC 122 sets it from MIDI, as the
-  specification has it): off, the panel's keys, knobs and PRESETS go to
-  MIDI out only. The engine keeps the knob positions it last took and
-  its patch, and a key let go still ends its note if it had started one
-  before. MIDI in still plays, so a sequencer can play the engine from
-  the panel's own notes. On again, the engine takes the panel's knobs
-  where they are.
-#### The settings and the screen
-`struct midi_settings` (version 2) adds the out channel (1 to 16), thru
-and local control after M6a's fields, all bytes, for M7 to save. The
-thru test build sets thru on and the out channel to 2. The panel
-screen's bottom line shows them ("MIDI out ch 1  thru off  local on"),
-redrawn when they change.
-#### Figures (fwtest 0.5.0, through `FWTEST_IMAGE` before its pin)
-- **Latency** from a key going down to its note on's first start bit, 20
-  keys: 3.260 to 5.286 ms, mean 4.196: the key's debounce (2.5 to 4.5 ms,
-  M3), then up to a block until the engine takes the event; the byte
-  starts in that block.
-- **The burst** (94 messages in one block): 28 merged, 18 dropped (the 10
-  note ons past the room, 6 more and the controller and bend to make room
-  for note offs), 16 note offs dropped with their note ons, none lost; 16
-  notes sent and each ended, 77 bytes in 10 transfers, 31 status bytes
-  left out.
-- **Cost at rest:** 1 863.9 instructions a block, 25 more than M6a's (the
-  two polls of an empty queue); loaded 110 207.6, +0.3% (the perf input's
-  keys and knobs now also go out). Code 20 144 bytes (+1 736), static RAM
-  143 776 (+520: the queue, the transfer buffer, the dropped-note bits,
-  the record).
-- **Never disturbs audio:** no underrun in any case, audiogold and fmgold
-  byte for byte as before.

+## 18. The UART on other JieLi chips (Q-12, Q-20)
+### HW-75: The UART as three other JieLi chips' open driver sets it up
+- Fact: Three other JieLi chips, the ones SDK63 calls br23, br25 and
+  bd29, have three UARTs with the FM-1's chip's eleven words in the same
+  order, widths and access (HW-68), at the same three bases, and SDK63's
+  drivers for them are open source. All three drivers do the same:
+  - The rate: `BAUD` is f / baud rounded to the nearest whole number,
+    divided by 4 (rounded down), less 1, where f is the UART clock; so
+    the rate is f / (4 × (`BAUD` + 1)). For 31 250 baud that is 383 from a
+    48 MHz clock and 191 from 24 MHz, both exact.
+  - Set-up: the pending flags cleared (`CON0` bits 13, 12 and 10 written
+    as 1) with bit 0 clear; then `BAUD`, and `OTCNT` when bit 5 is set;
+    then bit 0 set with the same three clears.
+  - `CON0` bit 1 set gives 9-bit frames, clear 8-bit.
+  - The receive ring: `RXSADR` its first byte and `RXEADR` one past its
+    last (the buffer's start plus its size); `RXCNT` the bytes per receive
+    pending; bits 6, 5 and 3 set together to receive by DMA.
+  - The idle timeout: `OTCNT` is the time in the low-speed bus clock
+    (milliseconds × that clock / 1000), not in the UART clock.
+  - Receive without the DMA (bit 6 clear): wait for bit 14, read `BUF`,
+    then write bit 12. The drivers only poll for such a byte, never take
+    it by interrupt.
+  - The receive and timeout interrupts write bit 7, then 10, then 12, and
+    then read `HRXCNT`; the driver's comment says the order must not
+    change.
+  - Transmit: a byte by writing `BUF`, waiting for bit 15 and clearing it
+    with bit 13; a DMA by clearing bit 13, setting bit 2 (the transmit
+    interrupt, taken when bits 2 and 15 are set), then writing `TXADR` and
+    then `TXCNT`.
+  - `CON0` bits 4, 8 and 9 are never used, and no error flag (framing,
+    overrun, parity) is read or cleared.
+  On br23's UART1 only, `CON1` holds hardware flow control: bit 0 turns
+  RTS on and bit 2 CTS, and bit 4 sets the RTS line by hand; when bit 0 is
+  set, each receive or timeout interrupt also writes bit 13; while bits 2
+  and 15 are set the sender waits, writing bit 14 (by that use, 15 is CTS
+  holding the sender off and 14 clears it). Where the bits overlap the FM-1's
+  chip's (`CON0` bits 0, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 10 to 15: HW-69, HW-70, HW-73)
+  they mean the same. But the chips differ: br23's clock header encodes
+  the UART clock in `CLK_CON1` bits 10-11 as 0 the PLL's 48 MHz, 1 the
+  oscillator, 2 the low-speed bus clock, while the FM-1's chip's SDK has
+  0 and 1 the other way round (HW-53). So none of this is confirmed for

+- Facts: HW-72 to HW-74 (the SMK-37's MIDI OUT is a UART's transmit side;
+  UART1 transmits by DMA, `TXADR` then `TXCNT`, and sets `CON0` bit 15
+  when the last byte has gone, cleared by writing bit 13; the FM-1 has no
+  MIDI OUT jack, so its bytes reach no socket); HARNESS.md's "MIDI
+  output" (`--midi-out`, a byte every 320 us). PROVENANCE P-50, and P-43
+  (the MIDI 1.0 specification) for the wire format, running status and
+  local control.
+- Sources: as M6a's; no other synthesizer's firmware and no MIDI
+  library's source was looked at.
+#### The path
+One context does everything: the engine's block callback. It polls the
+transmitter at the start of its events, takes the panel's events (and
+queues what they send), takes MIDI in (and queues what thru passes on),
+then polls again, so a message queued in a block has its first byte on
+the wire in that block if the wire is free. Nothing else writes the
+queue or the UART's transmit side, so there is no lock, and nothing ever
+waits for the wire: a poll that finds a transfer still running returns.
+#### The transmitter
+A poll sends only when the last transfer has gone (`CON0` bit 15,
+acknowledged with bit 13, every write keeping the UART and the receive
+DMA on), never while one runs, and a running transfer's 16-byte buffer
+is never touched. A transfer takes whole messages, up to 12 bytes (3.8
+ms), so under a long stream a new message waits at most that plus a
+block. No interrupt: the transmit interrupt's enable bit is known only
+from the emulator (HW-74), the receive side is polled the same way
+(M6a), and the polls a block gives are enough: the chunk lets the wire
+stay busy across a block. Polling costs throughput, though: a transfer
+can only start at a poll, so the wire idles from a transfer's end to
+the next poll; under a stream the wire carries about 88% of its 31 250
+baud (midiburst: 65 bytes in 23.6 ms). A full input wire passed on by
+thru therefore builds the queue up slowly, and the policy (below)
+applies. On the chip, what writing `CON0` during a transfer does beyond
+the acknowledge, and whether a pin carries UART1's transmit side at all,
+are open (Q-20); nothing here depends on the pin.
+#### Running status
+A channel message leaves out its status byte when it is the status sent
+last, while messages keep coming; when a poll finds the transfer done and
+nothing waiting, the wire has gone quiet and the next message carries its
+status, so a receiver connected meanwhile is never left without one.
+System common messages end running status, realtime messages don't. The
+panel's note offs are note ons at velocity 0 (the receiver treats both
+the same, M6a), so a run of notes keeps one status.
+#### The policy when the wire can't keep up
+The queue holds 32 messages (at most 96 bytes, 31 ms of the wire):
+- **Merging:** a control change, pitch bend, pressure or program change
+  replaces a waiting one of the same kind, channel (and controller or
+  note), looking back from the newest over such messages only, so no
+  value moves past a note, a mode message or a parameter-number sequence.
+  Data entry (6, 38), the parameter numbers (96 to 101) and the mode
+  messages (120 to 127) never merge: their order is their meaning.
+- **The reserve:** 8 places are kept for note offs (and all notes off,
+  all sound off). Any other message that finds the other 24 full is
+  dropped and counted.
+- **Never a stuck note:** a note on dropped marks its note, and its note
+  off is dropped too. A note off that finds all 32 full drops the newest
+  waiting message that ends no notes (a note on so dropped marks its
+  note). Only a queue of 32 note offs alone could lose one; it is counted.
+#### What the panel sends
+On the out channel (1 by default):
+- **Keys:** a note on at velocity 100 (the keys have no velocity) and a
+  note on at velocity 0 when let go, for the note the key started, so an
+  octave change while it is held can't leave it on. OCT- and OCT+ only
+  move the notes sent.
+- **KNOB1 to KNOB4:** as the first controllers M6a's map routes to them
+  (16 to 19 by default; a changed map changes them), each value the
+  inverse of how MIDI in reads it: the value nearest 64 whose offset is
+  the panel knob's position, held to the knob's span. So a far end with
+  its own knob at rest takes the position the panel's knob has; a value
+  is sent only when it changes. tools/midi_model.py checks every
+  position.
+- **PRESETS:** a program change, the test patch's number.
+- **SEL with MONO or POLY:** the mode messages 126 (value 1) and 127,
+  which MIDI in takes as mono and poly.
+- **Pitch:** the panel has no bend or pitch wheel; KNOB1 transposes and
+  goes as its controller (a bend could not carry ±24 semitones at the
+  default range of 2). Not sent: MASTER (the device's own output level,
+  not in the map), ALGORITHM (no controller in the map yet; M8), PLAY's
+  test tone, SELECT.
+#### Thru and local control
+- **Thru** (off by default) passes on every message MIDI in parsed, on
+  every channel, before the receive channel's filter, realtime and system
+  common included, as messages merged with the panel's at message
+  boundaries (never bytes, which would break running status). A SysEx is
+  not passed on: the parser keeps none of its bytes (M6a); it is counted.
+  Only bytes received at MIDI in go through thru, never the firmware's
+  own messages. A cable from out to in with thru on would repeat
+  messages without end, as on any instrument with soft thru.
+- **Local control** (on by default; CC 122 sets it from MIDI, as the
+  specification has it): off, the panel's keys, knobs and PRESETS go to
+  MIDI out only. The engine keeps the knob positions it last took and
+  its patch, and a key let go still ends its note if it had started one
+  before. MIDI in still plays, so a sequencer can play the engine from
+  the panel's own notes. On again, the engine takes the panel's knobs
+  where they are.
+#### The settings and the screen
+`struct midi_settings` (version 2) adds the out channel (1 to 16), thru
+and local control after M6a's fields, all bytes, for M7 to save. The
+thru test build sets thru on and the out channel to 2. The panel
+screen's bottom line shows them ("MIDI out ch 1  thru off  local on"),
+redrawn when they change.
+#### Figures (fwtest 0.5.0, through `FWTEST_IMAGE` before its pin)
+- **Latency** from a key going down to its note on's first start bit, 20
+  keys: 3.260 to 5.286 ms, mean 4.196: the key's debounce (2.5 to 4.5 ms,
+  M3), then up to a block until the engine takes the event; the byte
+  starts in that block.
+- **The burst** (94 messages in one block): 28 merged, 18 dropped (the 10
+  note ons past the room, 6 more and the controller and bend to make room
+  for note offs), 16 note offs dropped with their note ons, none lost; 16
+  notes sent and each ended, 77 bytes in 10 transfers, 31 status bytes
+  left out.

+  keys and knobs now also go out). Code 20 144 bytes (+1 736), static RAM
+  143 776 (+520: the queue, the transfer buffer, the dropped-note bits,
+  the record).
+- **Never disturbs audio:** no underrun in any case, audiogold and fmgold
+  byte for byte as before.

Claude may publish its own work without being asked, because artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared further: anything that imitates a real organization, person or record, and anything the person presented as sensitive. Claude builds those as files and lets the person decide whether they get a URL.

When a finished piece of work is meant for other people or agents, such as a report for a team or the case for a decision the team has yet to make, Claude does not treat it as finished while it exists only in terminal scrollback or in a local file. Claude publishes it, as an Artifact or through a first-party document connector when one is attached, and gives the person the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose. Claude publishes it even when the request is phrased as a question, such as "can you write up the plan?". When the request says who else will read or use the work, such as a team, a manager or a reviewer, or where it will be posted or presented, such as a channel or a meeting, Claude publishes it. A write-up that will be posted in a channel or a thread is still published, so the post can carry the link; when it is short, Claude also gives the text in its reply, ready to paste. When it might be passed along but nothing says so, Claude offers the page in one line instead of saying nothing. When the person asks only for Claude's own verdict, such as "should we ship this?", and names no one else who will read it, Claude gives the answer in the terminal and offers the page in one line instead of publishing it. A recommendation or analysis written up for someone else to act on is finished work for that reader, so Claude publishes it. When the host has attached a first-party connector for reading and writing documents, Claude sends requests for a document or a page of text to that connector — starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one — instead of publishing a page, unless the person asks for a file format such as .docx or .pptx. When the person asks for the file itself, such as "just give me the .html file" or "save these notes as a .md file", Claude gives them that file and does not publish it. Advice that the person will act on by themselves, right away, in the code they are working on is not meant for other people, so Claude does not need to publish it.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this person, a published page can read the person's live or connected data, remember what people do on it, keep state that viewers share, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question, store files people add, or give the viewer a file to save.
